Good evening, Ms. Ito. This is Claire from the front desk. I'm calling about your requests. First, we had the thermostat in your room checked by maintenance, and they repaired it, so the room should be warm in about twenty minutes. Second, your suit. We will have it pressed tonight, and it will be ready by seven a.m. We can bring it to your room, or you can pick it up at the front desk. And finally, you asked about the day of your check-out. No problem at all. We can have your bags stored until your train leaves. If you need anything else, please dial nine. Have a good night, and good luck at the fair tomorrow.

I have managed hotels for twenty years, and I can tell you what the perfect complaint sounds like. It has three steps. Step one: describe the problem in one sentence, without emotion. The room is cold, and the heating is not working. That's it. Step two: ask for one clear solution. Could you have someone check it, or could I change rooms? When guests ask for five things at once, we cannot help them fast. One problem, one solution. Step three: thank the person by name at the end. Thank you, Claire. It sounds small, but people remember it, and the next time you call, they will remember you. Angry guests usually get an apology. Calm guests usually get an upgrade.

First, I describe the problem in one calm sentence. Then, I say why it is important for me today. Next, I ask for one clear solution, like having the thermostat checked. After that, I confirm the time: by seven, or in ten minutes. Finally, I thank the person by name.
